concepts.label: Word Normalization: Stemming and Lemmatization
concepts.description: Stemming reduces words to root forms by cutting suffixes (e.g., 'skipping' → 'skip'), while lemmatization uses dictionary-based analysis to find base forms (e.g., 'am', 'are', 'is' → 'be').
coverage_criteria: Define stemming and lemmatization, and contrast one with the other with examples.

concepts.label: Linguistic Annotation: POS Tagging and Named Entity Recognition
concepts.description: POS tagging labels words with grammatical categories (noun, verb, etc.), while Named Entity Recognition identifies names, locations, and organizations in text.
coverage_criteria: Explain what POS tagging and Named Entity Recognition are, giving examples of each.

concepts.label: Machine Learning in NLP
concepts.description: After preprocessing, ML algorithms like Naive Bayes can be applied to tasks such as sentiment analysis, learning patterns from labeled data.
coverage_criteria: Describe the role of machine learning in NLP, giving Naive Bayes as an example.

concepts.label: NLP Definition and Suitability Criteria
concepts.description: Natural Language Processing (NLP) is a branch of artificial intelligence that uses machine learning to process and interpret texts and data. Three characteristics indicate when NLP is appropriate: the need to understand human communication, the requirement for the machine to respond with precision, and the ability to process and analyze large volumes of data for predictions or suggestions.
coverage_criteria: Define NLP as presented in the lesson.
List the three characteristics that make NLP suitable for problem-solving.
Give an example of a problem that would benefit from these characteristics.

concepts.label: Why Text Needs to Be Converted to Numbers for Machine Learning
concepts.description: Machine learning algorithms require numerical input (matrices). Text data must be vectorized into feature vectors so that models can learn a mapping Y=f(X).
coverage_criteria: Explain the necessity of numerical representation for ML models.
Describe the Y=f(X) formulation and the role of vectorization.

concepts.label: Rede Neural Artificial
concepts.description: Uma rede neural artificial é um modelo preditivo inspirado no cérebro, composto por neurônios artificiais conectados que realizam cálculos ponderados sobre as entradas e produzem saídas através de funções de ativação.
coverage_criteria: Definir o que é uma rede neural artificial e seus componentes principais (neurônios, conexões, função de ativação).
Descrever como um neurônio artificial calcula sua saída a partir das entradas, pesos e função de ativação.

concepts.label: Text Preprocessing: Segmentation, Tokenization, and Stop Words
concepts.description: The initial NLP steps: breaking documents into sentences (segmentation), sentences into words (tokenization), and removing common stop words to focus on meaningful content.
coverage_criteria: Explain segmentation, tokenization, and the role of stop words in NLP preprocessing.

concepts.label: Text Preprocessing: Tokenization and Stopword Removal
concepts.description: Tokenization splits text into individual words (tokens). Stopwords are common low-information words that are often removed to reduce noise and vocabulary size. NLTK provides built-in stopword lists.
coverage_criteria: Define tokenization and stopword removal.
Write code to remove stopwords using NLTK.

concepts.label: Tokenization with NLTK
concepts.description: Understanding tokenization as converting text into a list of words and punctuation, and using nltk.word_tokenize for better handling of contractions than simple regex splitting.
coverage_criteria: Recognizes that NLTK represents tokenized text as a list of string tokens.
Uses nltk.word_tokenize to split a sentence with contractions and explains why it is advantageous.

concepts.label: Handling Portuguese text encoding (ISO 8859-1)
concepts.description: Awareness that many Portuguese text resources use ISO 8859-1 encoding and how to decode such text in Python when reading files.
coverage_criteria: Explains why specifying encoding is necessary when opening Portuguese text files.
Decodes bytes using 'ISO 8859-1' encoding in Python.

concepts.label: Stop Words Removal
concepts.description: Filtering out common words (e.g., 'the', 'is') that carry little semantic value, using predefined lists such as NLTK's stopwords.
coverage_criteria: Identify common stop words.
Remove stop words from text using NLTK.

concepts.label: Word-level Tokenization
concepts.description: Splitting raw text into individual words (tokens) as the first step of NLP pipelines, often using functions like d2l.tokenize.
coverage_criteria: Tokenize a sentence into words.
Explain why tokenization is necessary.

concepts.label: Vocabulary Construction and Out-of-Vocabulary Handling
concepts.description: Building a vocabulary from training tokens with a minimum frequency filter, and ignoring unknown words during testing to avoid errors.
coverage_criteria: Create a vocabulary with frequency filters.
Explain the strategy for handling OOV words.

concepts.label: Expressões Regulares: Definição e Metacaracteres Básicos
concepts.description: Introduz expressões regulares como método para busca de padrões em textos e apresenta o conceito de metacaracteres, que são símbolos com significados especiais.
coverage_criteria: Definir o que é uma expressão regular.
Citar pelo menos três metacaracteres e explicar brevemente sua função.

concepts.label: Metacaracteres Representantes: Ponto, Lista e Lista Negada
concepts.description: Descreve os metacaracteres representantes: ponto (.) que representa qualquer caractere, lista ([...]) que busca um dos caracteres listados e lista negada ([^...]) que busca caracteres que não estão na lista.
coverage_criteria: Explicar o que o ponto, a lista e a lista negada representam em uma regex.
Dado um texto, escrever uma regex que utilize lista para buscar palavras com um conjunto específico de caracteres.

concepts.label: Metacaracteres Quantificadores
concepts.description: Apresenta os quantificadores: asterisco (*) para zero ou mais, opcional (?) para zero ou uma, mais (+) para uma ou mais e chaves ({x,y}) para um número específico de repetições, com exemplos usando classes de caracteres.
coverage_criteria: Diferenciar o uso de *, + e ? com exemplos.
Escrever uma regex utilizando {x,y} para limitar repetições.

concepts.label: Âncoras: Circunflexo e Cifrão
concepts.description: Explica que o circunflexo (^) ancora a busca no início da linha/string e o cifrão ($) no final, destacando que ^ dentro de colchetes tem função de negação.
coverage_criteria: Explicar a função das âncoras ^ e $.
Escrever uma regex que encontre uma palavra no início de uma linha e outra no final.

concepts.label: Alternação e Agrupamento
concepts.description: Mostra o uso do pipe (|) para alternância (OU) e dos parênteses ( ) para agrupar partes da regex, permitindo construir padrões com múltiplas opções.
coverage_criteria: Utilizar | e () para criar uma regex que capture uma entre várias palavras.
Diferenciar (rato|Roma) de [rato|Roma].

concepts.label: Escapando Metacaracteres
concepts.description: Ensina que a contrabarra (\) é usada para tratar metacaracteres como literais, por exemplo, \. para um ponto literal ou \( para parênteses literal.
coverage_criteria: Identificar em uma regex quais caracteres estão escapados e por quê.
Escrever uma regex que encontre um parêntese literal em um texto.

concepts.label: Classes de Caracteres por Atalho
concepts.description: Apresenta os atalhos \d (dígito), \w (alfanumérico), \s (espaçamento) e suas negações \D, \W, \S, que simplificam a construção de padrões comuns.
coverage_criteria: Substituir [0-9] por \d em uma regex.
Explicar a diferença entre \w e \W.

concepts.label: Métodos Básicos do Módulo re do Python
concepts.description: Explora os métodos principais do módulo re do Python: match(), search(), findall() para busca de padrões, e split(), sub(), group() para manipulação de strings.
coverage_criteria: Usar re.search para encontrar a primeira ocorrência de um padrão.
Aplicar re.sub para substituir um padrão em um texto.
Extrair subgrupos de um match com group().

concepts.label: Aplicações Práticas de Regex
concepts.description: Ilustra casos reais de uso de expressões regulares: extração de e-mails, números de telefone, divisão de frases, detecção de acrônimos e validação de formatos como datas e IPs.
coverage_criteria: Explicar como uma regex pode validar um formato de data.
Modificar uma regex de extração de e-mail para incluir um domínio específico.
Escrever código Python que usa split para separar frases.

concepts.label: Regex em JavaScript
concepts.description: Mostra como expressões regulares são criadas em JavaScript usando barras como delimitadores, com exemplo de negação de números.
coverage_criteria: Escrever uma regex simples em JavaScript.
Explicar a diferença entre usar barras e aspas.

concepts.label: Similaridade Léxica
concepts.description: Define similaridade léxica como a medida de sobreposição de palavras ou caracteres entre dois fragmentos de texto, sem considerar significado, e discute os níveis de granularidade (caractere, palavra, frase).
coverage_criteria: Explicar o que é similaridade léxica e dar um exemplo.
Diferenciar similaridade em nível de caractere e de palavra.

concepts.label: Distância de Edição Mínima e Levenshtein
concepts.description: Apresenta a distância de edição mínima como o número mínimo de operações (inserção, deleção, substituição) para transformar uma string em outra, e a variante Levenshtein onde a substituição custa 2.
coverage_criteria: Calcular a distância de edição mínima entre duas strings.
Computar a distância de Levenshtein e explicar a diferença de custo.

concepts.label: Similaridade de Jaccard
concepts.description: Mede a similaridade entre dois conjuntos calculando a interseção dividida pela união, resultando em um valor entre 0 e 1, com exemplos em Python.
coverage_criteria: Calcular a similaridade de Jaccard para dois conjuntos de palavras.
Interpretar o resultado próximo de 1 ou de 0.

concepts.label: Similaridade de Cosseno
concepts.description: Calcula a similaridade entre dois vetores de frequência de palavras usando o cosseno do ângulo entre eles, com implementação em Python.
coverage_criteria: Calcular a similaridade de cosseno entre dois textos usando frequências de palavras.
Explicar por que o valor varia entre -1 e 1.

concepts.label: Classificação de Algoritmos de Similaridade de Strings
concepts.description: Categoriza os algoritmos de similaridade em baseados em caracteres (ex.: Levenshtein) e baseados em termos (ex.: cosseno, Jaccard), indicando quando cada um é mais adequado.
coverage_criteria: Listar exemplos de algoritmos baseados em caracteres e baseados em termos.
Explicar em que situação um é preferível ao outro.

concepts.label: Aplicações de Similaridade Textual
concepts.description: Lista e exemplifica aplicações reais de medidas de similaridade: sistemas de busca, recomendação, correção ortográfica, autocomplete, sumarização e detecção de duplicatas.
coverage_criteria: Citar ao menos três aplicações de similaridade textual.
Explicar como a similaridade ajuda em uma dessas aplicações.

concepts.label: Similaridade Semântica e Diferenciação da Léxica
concepts.description: Define similaridade semântica como a que considera o significado das palavras em contexto, contrastando com a léxica, e fornece exemplos como 'carro' e 'automóvel'.
coverage_criteria: Diferenciar similaridade semântica de léxica com exemplos.
Explicar por que a semântica é mais difícil de computar.

concepts.label: Abordagens para Similaridade Semântica: Baseadas em Conhecimento e Corpus
concepts.description: Descreve as duas principais abordagens para calcular similaridade semântica: baseada em corpus (grandes bases de texto) e baseada em conhecimento (redes semânticas como WordNet).
coverage_criteria: Distinguir as abordagens baseada em conhecimento e baseada em corpus.
Dar um exemplo de recurso usado em cada abordagem.

concepts.label: WordNet e Relações Semânticas
concepts.description: Apresenta a WordNet como um banco de dados lexical que organiza palavras em synsets e inclui relações semânticas como sinonímia, antonímia, meronímia, holonímia, hiponímia, hiperonímia, homonímia e polissemia.
coverage_criteria: Explicar o que é um synset na WordNet.
Definir e exemplificar pelo menos três relações semânticas (ex.: hiponímia, meronímia).

concepts.label: Path Similarity e Lowest Common Subsumer (LCS)
concepts.description: Explica a similaridade de caminho (Path Similarity) como 1/(distância + 1) em uma taxonomia, e o LCS como o ancestral comum mais específico, ambos usando a WordNet.
coverage_criteria: Calcular a Path Similarity entre dois conceitos em uma hierarquia.
Identificar o LCS de dois conceitos em uma taxonomia.

concepts.label: Acesso à WordNet com NLTK (Inglês e Português)
concepts.description: Demonstra como acessar a WordNet em Python usando a biblioteca NLTK, incluindo suporte para português via Open Multilingual Wordnet (lang='por'), embora as definições estejam em inglês.
coverage_criteria: Escrever um script Python que recupera synsets de uma palavra inglesa no NLTK.
Recuperar synsets de uma palavra em português e discutir limitações.

concepts.label: BOW Vectorization Process
concepts.description: The BOW vectorization process consists of determining the vocabulary (collecting unique words) and then counting the occurrences of each vocabulary word in each document to produce a count vector.
coverage_criteria: List the steps for BOW vectorization (vocabulary construction and counting).
Apply counting to convert a small document into a BOW vector.

concepts.label: Loss of Word Order and Context in BOW
concepts.description: BOW discards the order of words, meaning it cannot capture syntax or semantics that depend on word sequence. This loss of contextual information is a fundamental limitation of the model.
coverage_criteria: State that BOW does not preserve word order.
Provide an example of how meaning can be lost due to ignoring word order.

concepts.label: Implementing BOW with Keras Tokenizer
concepts.description: In Python, the Keras Tokenizer class can be used to implement BOW. After fitting on texts to build the vocabulary, texts_to_matrix with mode='count' generates count vectors.
coverage_criteria: Write Python code to use Keras Tokenizer for BOW vectorization.
Explain the roles of fit_on_texts and texts_to_matrix.

concepts.label: Applications and Strengths of BOW
concepts.description: Despite its simplicity, BOW is effective for tasks like text classification and profanity detection. Its strengths are simplicity and low computational cost.
coverage_criteria: Name two NLP applications where BOW is useful.
Explain why BOW's simplicity can be advantageous.

concepts.label: Sparse Vectors Problem
concepts.description: When the vocabulary is large, BOW vectors become mostly zeros (sparse), leading to high memory usage and computational inefficiency.
coverage_criteria: Define a sparse vector in the context of BOW.
Explain why sparsity is a challenge for machine learning.

concepts.label: Implementing BOW from Scratch in Python
concepts.description: BOW can be implemented manually by writing functions to tokenize, remove stopwords, build a vocabulary, and generate count vectors using basic Python and NumPy.
coverage_criteria: Describe the key components of a from-scratch BOW implementation.
Write a simple function to generate a BOW vector from text.

concepts.label: N-gram Extension to Bag-of-Words
concepts.description: BOW can be extended to n-grams (e.g., bigrams) where tokens are sequences of n consecutive words, partially capturing word order.
coverage_criteria: Define an n-gram and give an example of bigrams.
Explain how n-grams address the loss-of-order limitation.

concepts.label: Binary Bag-of-Words Encoding
concepts.description: In binary BOW, a sentence is represented by a binary vector where each dimension indicates the presence (1) or absence (0) of a vocabulary word, rather than its count.
coverage_criteria: Differentiate between count-based and binary BOW.
Given a vocabulary and a sentence, produce a binary BOW vector.

concepts.label: HashVectorizer: Hashing-based Vectorization
concepts.description: Scikit-learn's HashVectorizer applies a hash function to map terms to numerical indices, saving memory but making it impossible to recover original feature names, unlike CountVectorizer.
coverage_criteria: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using HashVectorizer compared to CountVectorizer.

concepts.label: Bag-of-Words Representation
concepts.description: The bag-of-words model represents text as a vector of word frequencies, ignoring word order. It converts unstructured text into numerical features using a vocabulary of the most frequent words.
coverage_criteria: Explain the bag-of-words assumption (ignoring word order).
Create a BoW vector from tokenized text and a vocabulary.
Describe how to select the vocabulary size (e.g., top N words).

concepts.label: Limitações do TF-IDF
concepts.description: O TF-IDF pondera frequência de termos pela inversa da frequência nos documentos, mas produz vetores esparsos de alta dimensionalidade que não capturam semântica complexa.
coverage_criteria: Defina TF-IDF e explique por que é menos eficaz que word embeddings para similaridade semântica.

concepts.label: Bag of Words (BoW)
concepts.description: A text representation that counts word occurrences in a document, ignoring order but preserving multiplicity, often forming a document-term matrix.
coverage_criteria: Create a BoW vector for a given document.
Explain the main limitation of BoW (ignoring word order).
Describe the document-term matrix structure.

concepts.label: Count-Based Text Representations and Limitations
concepts.description: Bag-of-Words and TF-IDF represent text by counting words (or n-grams) and weighting them by importance. Preprocessing steps like stemming and stop-word removal are common. These methods yield sparse vectors that ignore word context and cannot handle unknown words.
coverage_criteria: Compute Bag-of-Words and TF-IDF vectors for a small corpus.
List at least two limitations of count-based representations.
Explain the purpose of stemming and stop-word removal in text preprocessing.

concepts.label: Word Embeddings as Dense Vectors
concepts.description: Unlike sparse encodings, word embeddings are dense numerical vectors where each dimension captures latent features. They are lower-dimensional than the vocabulary and enable models to process semantic meaning efficiently.
coverage_criteria: Define word embeddings and contrast them with sparse representations.
Explain why dense vectors are more efficient than one-hot vectors.

concepts.label: TF-IDF Output: Document Vectors and Applications
concepts.description: After computing TF-IDF for all terms, each document is represented as a weighted term vector, where high weights indicate discriminative terms. These document vectors are used in data mining tasks such as classification, clustering, and information retrieval, especially document search.
coverage_criteria: Explain how TF-IDF transforms documents into feature vectors.
List at least three applications of TF-IDF in text analysis.

concepts.label: TF-IDF Discriminative Power and Comparison with Bag of Words
concepts.description: TF-IDF assigns higher weights to terms that appear frequently in a specific document but rarely across the corpus, making them discriminative features. A term that appears in every document gets IDF=0 and thus TF-IDF=0, meaning it has no discriminative power. This contrasts with Bag of Words, which merely counts occurrences and does not differentiate important terms from common ones.
coverage_criteria: Explain why a word with IDF=0 is not useful for distinguishing documents.
Describe the key difference between Bag of Words and TF-IDF.

concepts.label: Loading and exploring NLTK's Portuguese text corpora
concepts.description: How to import and access NLTK's built-in Portuguese corpora, including the examples module, Machado de Assis works, and the MacMorpho tagged corpus, to retrieve text, words, and tagged words.
coverage_criteria: Imports a Portuguese corpus like nltk.corpus.machado.
Lists file IDs and retrieves raw text or words for a file.
For MacMorpho, accesses tagged_words and distinguishes between words and tagged tokens.

concepts.label: Working with the Floresta treebank
concepts.description: How to access the Floresta Portuguese treebank, simplify its complex part-of-speech tags, and retrieve parsed syntactic trees.
coverage_criteria: Imports nltk.corpus.floresta and lists words or tagged words.
Writes a function to simplify tags (e.g., 'H+n' to 'n').
Accesses parsed_sents() and can explain that they represent syntactic structure.

concepts.label: Searching text with NLTK's built-in and regex methods
concepts.description: Using NLTK's concordance, similar, collocations, and findall with regex to locate words and analyze their contexts.
coverage_criteria: Uses concordance() to display a word in context.
Uses similar() to find words with similar distribution.
Uses collocations() to extract frequent multi-word expressions.
Applies findall() with a regex pattern to search text.

concepts.label: Analyzing tokenized text with NLTK and Python
concepts.description: Performing basic text analysis operations on tokenized lists, including extracting unique vocabulary, filtering/transforming tokens with list comprehensions, computing frequency distributions, and finding n-grams containing a target word.
coverage_criteria: Uses set() and sorted() to obtain the unique vocabulary of a tokenized text.
Writes a list comprehension to filter tokens by length or case.
Creates a FreqDist and retrieves the most frequent words.
Generates n-grams and filters those containing a specific word, displaying the most frequent.

concepts.label: Implementing a custom concordance tool
concepts.description: Writing a Python function that searches for a word in a list of sentences and prints it with surrounding context, mimicking NLTK's concordance.
coverage_criteria: Defines a function that takes a word and context width, iterates over tokenized sentences, and prints formatted concordance lines.

concepts.label: Stemming with Porter Stemmer in NLTK
concepts.description: Using the Porter Stemmer algorithm to reduce words to their stems through rule-based suffix stripping.
coverage_criteria: Applies PorterStemmer to a list of words and observes the stemmed outputs.
Explains that stemmed outputs may not be real words (e.g., 'generously' -> 'gener').

concepts.label: Snowball Stemmer for multilingual stemming
concepts.description: Snowball Stemmer is a stemming algorithm supporting multiple languages, often more accurate than Porter Stemmer. Use it to reduce words to their stems.
coverage_criteria: List several languages supported by SnowballStemmer.
Initialize SnowballStemmer with a language and stem a word.
Explain why Snowball Stemmer might be preferred over Porter Stemmer.

concepts.label: Lemmatization with WordNetLemmatizer
concepts.description: WordNetLemmatizer reduces words to dictionary form using WordNet. Unlike stemming, lemmas are actual words. Requires downloading wordnet corpus.
coverage_criteria: Explain the difference between lemmatization and stemming.
Instantiate WordNetLemmatizer and lemmatize a word.
Identify that lemmatization depends on a lexical database like WordNet.

concepts.label: Processing text and exploring documents, tokens, and spans in spaCy
concepts.description: Use spacy.blank to create a pipeline and process text into a Doc. Understand tokenization as the process of splitting text into tokens. Access tokens by index and create spans.
coverage_criteria: Write code to create a blank Portuguese pipeline, process 'Olá mundo', and confirm the result is a Doc.
Given a Doc for 'três cachorros e dois gatos', retrieve the first token and create a span for 'três cachorros'.
Define tokenization and explain that spaCy's tokenizer is language-specific, giving examples.

concepts.label: Using lexical attributes for pattern detection
concepts.description: Token attributes like `like_num` can identify numeric tokens. Combine attributes to find patterns such as percentages.
coverage_criteria: Explain how to find tokens that represent numbers using `like_num`.
Write a loop to detect a number followed by a '%' sign.

concepts.label: Loading and understanding pre-trained spaCy models
concepts.description: Load pre-trained pipelines with spacy.load. Understand model packages (config, weights, strings.json) and trade-offs between blank and pre-trained models of different sizes.
coverage_criteria: Write code to load the Portuguese small pipeline and process a text, printing the Doc's text.
List what is included in a spaCy pipeline package and explain why training data is not needed.
Explain the difference between blank and pre-trained models, and compare speed/accuracy trade-offs of model sizes.

concepts.label: Predicting part-of-speech tags and dependencies
concepts.description: After processing text with a trained pipeline, each token has a .pos_ (coarse POS tag) and .dep_ (dependency label).
coverage_criteria: Given a Doc from a Portuguese pipeline, write a loop to print each token's text, .pos_, and .dep_.

concepts.label: Named entity recognition and manual correction
concepts.description: Trained pipelines identify named entities (doc.ents). When predictions miss an entity, manually create a Span for the missed tokens.
coverage_criteria: Iterate over doc.ents printing entity text and label, and use spacy.explain to describe a label.
When a model fails to recognize 'iPhone X', write code to create a Span for those two tokens.

concepts.label: Rule-based matching with Matcher
concepts.description: Use the Matcher class to define token-based patterns with attributes and operators for finding sequences in text.
coverage_criteria: Write code to initialize a Matcher, add a pattern that matches 'iPhone X', apply it to a Doc, and print matched spans.
Write patterns using lemmas, POS tags, and quantifiers (e.g., '+', '*', '?') to match flexible sequences.

concepts.label: Overview of spaCy as a production-ready NLP library
concepts.description: spaCy is an open-source MIT-licensed NLP library, maintained by Explosion.ai, supporting 73 languages and focused on production with pre-trained models.
coverage_criteria: Identify spaCy as a production-focused NLP library.
Differentiate spaCy from other libraries like NLTK (academic).
State that it supports multiple languages and offers small, medium, and large pre-trained models.

concepts.label: Contêineres spaCy: Doc, Token e Span
concepts.description: No spaCy, um Doc representa o documento inteiro processado, contendo uma sequência de objetos Token. Um Span é uma fatia de um Doc. Esses contêineres são a base para navegar e acessar atributos linguísticos.
coverage_criteria: Explicar o que é um Doc e como criá-lo.
Descrever Token como uma unidade individual com atributos.
Demonstrar como criar um Span usando slicing.

concepts.label: Atributos de tokens no spaCy: text, shape_ e is_alpha
concepts.description: Cada token possui atributos como .text, .shape_ e .is_alpha que descrevem sua forma e tipo, permitindo filtrar ou identificar padrões no texto.
coverage_criteria: Listar e definir os atributos text, shape_ e is_alpha.
Fornecer um exemplo de uso de shape_.
Usar is_alpha para separar palavras de pontuação ou números.

concepts.label: POS tagging – classificação gramatical dos tokens
concepts.description: POS tagging atribui a cada token uma classe gramatical (ex.: substantivo, verbo). No spaCy, usa-se .pos_ (como NOUN, VERB) e .tag_ para detalhes mais granulares.
coverage_criteria: Explicar o que é POS tagging.
Extrair tags POS de uma frase com .pos_.
Identificar tags como PROPN, VERB em exemplos.

concepts.label: Lematização – redução à forma canônica
concepts.description: Lematização transforma palavras flexionadas em sua forma base (ex.: 'faz' → 'fazer'). No spaCy, acessa-se via .lemma_. Diferencia-se de stemming, que apenas corta radicais.
coverage_criteria: Definir lematização e diferenciar de stemming.
Obter o lema de um token com .lemma_.
Dar um exemplo de lematização como 'comprou' → 'comprar'.

concepts.label: Análise de dependências sintáticas (dep_)
concepts.description: A análise de dependências atribui a cada token um rótulo .dep_ indicando sua função sintática (ex.: nsubj para sujeito, obj para objeto). Permite visualizar a estrutura da frase com displacy.
coverage_criteria: Explicar o que .dep_ representa.
Identificar o nsubj de um verbo em uma frase.
Usar displacy.render para visualizar dependências.

concepts.label: Reconhecimento de Entidades Nomeadas (NER) no spaCy
concepts.description: NER identifica entidades como pessoas, organizações, locais no texto. No spaCy, acessível via doc.ents, com atributos como .label_ (PERSON, ORG, etc.).
coverage_criteria: Definir NER e listar tipos de entidades.
Extrair entidades com doc.ents.
Imprimir texto e label de cada entidade.

concepts.label: Probability Foundations for Naive Bayes
concepts.description: Foundational probability concepts: basic probability, conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B), and Bayes theorem P(B|A) = P(A|B)P(B)/P(A) with posterior, likelihood, prior, and evidence.
coverage_criteria: State the formula for conditional probability.
Write Bayes theorem and name the terms.
Compute a simple probability using the formula.

concepts.label: Feature Independence Assumption and Multicollinearity
concepts.description: Naive Bayes assumes features are independent given the class (the 'naive' assumption). Multicollinearity (high feature correlation) violates this independence, causing poor performance.
coverage_criteria: Explain the naive independence assumption.
Define multicollinearity and its impact on Naive Bayes.
Describe a method to detect multicollinearity.

concepts.label: Naive Bayes Variants: Bernoulli, Multinomial, Gaussian
concepts.description: Three main variants: Bernoulli for binary features, Multinomial for discrete counts (especially text), and Gaussian for continuous features assuming a normal distribution.
coverage_criteria: Match each variant to its typical data type.
Identify the appropriate variant for a given scenario.
Recognize scikit-learn class names for each variant.

concepts.label: Practical Aspects of Naive Bayes: Applications, Advantages, and Usage
concepts.description: Naive Bayes is used in text classification, sentiment analysis, recommendation, and real-time prediction. Advantages: fast, less training data (when independent), good with categorical/text data. Disadvantages: independence assumption, zero frequency. Best when features are fairly independent and for text tasks.
coverage_criteria: List at least three real-world applications.
State two advantages and two disadvantages.
Describe scenarios where Naive Bayes is a good choice or should be avoided.

concepts.label: Improving Naive Bayes Performance
concepts.description: Techniques include removing correlated features, feature engineering, domain knowledge, using probabilistic features, Laplace smoothing, and the log-trick for numerical stability: argmax (log prior + Σ log P(xᵢ|y)).
coverage_criteria: Name at least three improvement strategies.
Explain why the log-trick is used.
Apply the log-trick in a posterior calculation.

concepts.label: Gaussian Naive Bayes: Prior, Likelihood, and PDF
concepts.description: In Gaussian Naive Bayes, the prior P(y) is the class frequency. The class conditional probability P(xᵢ|y) is modeled with a Gaussian PDF: (1/√(2πσ²)) exp(-(x-μ)²/(2σ²)), where μ and σ² are estimated per feature per class.
coverage_criteria: Calculate prior probabilities from a dataset.
Write the Gaussian PDF formula.
Compute a PDF value given mean and variance.

concepts.label: Naive Bayes Training and Prediction Procedure
concepts.description: Training: compute per-class means, variances, and prior probabilities. Prediction: choose the class with the highest log-posterior: log P(y) + Σ log P(xᵢ|y) using argmax.
coverage_criteria: List the statistics computed during training.
Explain the prediction step using argmax.
Perform a simple prediction by hand for a small dataset.

concepts.label: Implementing Naive Bayes in Python
concepts.description: The classifier is implemented as a Python class with fit() and predict() methods, using NumPy arrays, storing learned parameters as attributes. Model performance is evaluated using accuracy on a test set.
coverage_criteria: Describe the class structure and key methods (fit, predict).
Explain how accuracy is computed and interpreted.
Identify the attributes stored after training (e.g., means, variances, priors).

concepts.label: Sentiment Analysis: Definition and Supervised Learning
concepts.description: Sentiment analysis classifies text as positive or negative based on sentiment-bearing words. It is a supervised classification task that requires labeled data for training.
coverage_criteria: Define sentiment analysis.
Explain why labeled data is necessary for supervised sentiment analysis.
Give examples of positive and negative cue words.

concepts.label: Derivation of Naive Bayes Decision Rule
concepts.description: The step-by-step derivation from Bayes theorem to the final classification formula: select class c that maximizes P(c) * ∏ P(word|c).
coverage_criteria: Write the final decision rule formula.
Explain the steps: posterior maximization, dropping the denominator, independence assumption.

concepts.label: Naive Bayes Training: Prior and Likelihood Computation
concepts.description: How to compute prior class probabilities P(c) = Nc/N and word likelihoods P(word|c) as relative frequency in class c.
coverage_criteria: Calculate prior from class counts.
Calculate word likelihoods from training documents.

concepts.label: Logarithmic Transformation for Numerical Stability
concepts.description: Using the log of the Naive Bayes product to convert it into a sum, preventing underflow from multiplying many small probabilities.
coverage_criteria: Explain why log-sum avoids underflow.
Transform a product expression into a log-sum.

concepts.label: Stemming
concepts.description: Reducing words to their root form (e.g., 'running' → 'run') to consolidate terms, using algorithms like SnowballStemmer from NLTK.
coverage_criteria: Explain the purpose of stemming.
Apply a stemmer to a list of words.

concepts.label: Binary Multinomial Naive Bayes
concepts.description: A variant that uses binary features (word presence/absence) instead of word counts, emphasizing occurrence over frequency.
coverage_criteria: Contrast binary and frequency-based Naive Bayes.
Explain when binary features might be useful.

concepts.label: Aplicação do Multinomial Naive Bayes em scikit-learn
concepts.description: Implementação prática do classificador MultinomialNB para análise de sentimento ou detecção de spam, incluindo preparação dos dados e treinamento.
coverage_criteria: Justificar a escolha do MultinomialNB para dados de contagem de palavras.
Carregar e pré-processar um dataset de texto para classificação.
Treinar um modelo MultinomialNB e fazer predições.

concepts.label: Métricas de avaliação para classificação
concepts.description: Métricas derivadas da matriz de confusão: acurácia, precisão, recall, F1-score, para avaliar o desempenho de classificadores binários.
coverage_criteria: Definir matriz de confusão e os termos VP, FP, VN, FN.
Calcular acurácia, precisão, recall e F1-score a partir da matriz.
Interpretar o significado de cada métrica.

concepts.label: Ajuste de hiperparâmetros com GridSearchCV
concepts.description: Busca exaustiva dos melhores hiperparâmetros usando validação cruzada para otimizar o desempenho do classificador Naive Bayes.
coverage_criteria: Explicar o propósito do ajuste de hiperparâmetros.
Diferenciar Grid Search de Random Search.
Aplicar GridSearchCV no scikit-learn para encontrar os melhores parâmetros.

concepts.label: Distribuição de classes desbalanceada
concepts.description: Identificação de conjuntos de dados com desproporção entre classes e compreensão de seu impacto na classificação.
coverage_criteria: Reconhecer um dataset desbalanceado a partir da distribuição de rótulos.
Discutir por que dados desbalanceados podem ser problemáticos.
Mencionar possíveis estratégias de mitigação.

concepts.label: Incorporação 2D Simplificada para Visualizar Similaridade
concepts.description: É possível construir word embeddings bidimensionais atribuindo manualmente pontuações (ex.: fofura e tamanho) para animais, de modo que palavras similares fiquem próximas no espaço vetorial, ilustrando o princípio da similaridade semântica por proximidade espacial.
coverage_criteria: Dado um plot 2D de animais com escores de atributos, identifique os mais similares.
Explique como a distância euclidiana mede similaridade em um embedding 2D.

concepts.label: Alta Dimensionalidade dos Embeddings Reais e Redução de Dimensionalidade
concepts.description: Modelos word2vec reais usam centenas de dimensões (100-300) para capturar relações semânticas complexas, impossibilitando visualização direta; técnicas como t-SNE ou PCA são necessárias para projetar em 2D.
coverage_criteria: Explique por que embeddings reais são de alta dimensionalidade.
Cite uma técnica para visualizar embeddings de alta dimensionalidade.

concepts.label: Treinamento do Word2Vec e Amostragem Negativa
concepts.description: O treinamento do Word2Vec maximiza a probabilidade de pares palavra-contexto usando uma função softmax; para reduzir custo, a amostragem negativa gera exemplos negativos, otimizando o cálculo.
coverage_criteria: Explique o objetivo de treinamento do Word2Vec.
Qual o propósito da amostragem negativa?

concepts.label: Comparação entre Word2Vec, GloVe e fastText
concepts.description: Word2Vec foca em contexto local, GloVe utiliza estatísticas globais de co-ocorrência, e fastText usa subword n-grams para representar palavras desconhecidas, oferecendo diferentes trade-offs.
coverage_criteria: Compare Word2Vec, GloVe e fastText em termos de contexto e tratamento de palavras desconhecidas.

concepts.label: fastText: Subword Embeddings
concepts.description: fastText represents each word as the sum of its character n‑gram embeddings, allowing it to build vectors for out‑of‑vocabulary words and handle morphologically rich languages.
coverage_criteria: Explain how fastText’s subword approach addresses the out‑of‑vocabulary problem.
Describe the difference between Word2vec and fastText regarding word representation.

concepts.label: Word2Vec
concepts.description: A shallow neural network model that learns word embeddings from large corpora using either the Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW) or skip-gram architecture.
coverage_criteria: Distinguish between CBOW and skip-gram training objectives.
Explain how Word2Vec produces dense vectors for words.
Describe a practical use of pre-trained Word2Vec embeddings.

concepts.label: Count-based Word Vector Construction and Dimensionality Reduction
concepts.description: Word vectors can be built by counting word co-occurrences in contexts from a corpus. This yields high-dimensional vectors that often contain redundant information; dimensionality reduction techniques like SVD compress them into a smaller, more manageable number of dimensions (e.g., 100-300).
coverage_criteria: Construct a simple co-occurrence matrix from a small corpus.
Explain why raw co-occurrence vectors can be too high-dimensional.
Name dimensionality reduction as a solution and state typical reduced dimensions.

concepts.label: Semantic and Syntactic Relationships in Word2Vec Embeddings
concepts.description: Word2Vec embeddings capture a variety of linguistic relationships, including verb tenses, capital-country associations, and gender pairs, by encoding them as consistent vector offsets.
coverage_criteria: Provide at least two distinct types of linguistic relationships that word vectors can capture (e.g., tense, geography).
Explain why such relationships emerge from the training objective.

concepts.label: Word Embeddings as Neural Network Weights
concepts.description: In Word2Vec, the word embeddings are the learned weights connecting the one-hot input to the hidden layer (or hidden to output, depending on architecture).
coverage_criteria: Indicate that after training, the embedding for a word is extracted from the weight matrix of the neural network.

concepts.label: Semantic Similarity and Properties of Embedding Space
concepts.description: In a distributional framework, words are similar if they share similar contexts. Embedding vectors place these words in a space where distance (e.g., cosine) reflects similarity. Well‑trained embeddings also exhibit clustering of related words and support analogical reasoning (e.g., king - man + woman ≈ queen).
coverage_criteria: Explain how word similarity is defined by context rather than spelling.
Given a 2D plot, identify which words are most similar based on distance.
Describe the analogy property of ideal embeddings with an example.

concepts.label: Training a Custom Embedding Layer
concepts.description: A neural network can include an embedding layer initialized randomly and trained end‑to‑end for a specific task, producing specialized word representations. This requires large amounts of data.
coverage_criteria: Describe how a custom embedding layer is trained within a model.
State one advantage and one disadvantage of training embeddings from scratch.

concepts.label: Using Pre‑trained Word Embeddings
concepts.description: Pre‑trained word vectors can be used in two ways: as static features (fixed during downstream training) or fine‑tuned (adjusted to the task). The Gensim library provides convenient access to pre‑trained models (Word2vec, GloVe, fastText) and similarity operations.
coverage_criteria: List and describe the two modes of using pre‑trained embeddings.
Write code to load a pre‑trained model from Gensim and find similar words.

concepts.label: Documento, Corpus e Streaming no Gensim
concepts.description: No Gensim, um documento é uma sequência de texto (str), um corpus é uma coleção de documentos para treinamento não supervisionado, e o streaming permite processar grandes corpora sem carregar tudo em memória.
coverage_criteria: Defina documento e corpus no Gensim.
Explique como o Gensim lida com grandes conjuntos de dados usando streaming.

concepts.label: Modelos no Gensim como Transformações
concepts.description: Um modelo no Gensim aprende uma transformação entre espaços vetoriais (ex.: BOW para TF-IDF) a partir de um corpus de treinamento e pode ser aplicado a novos documentos.
coverage_criteria: Defina o papel de um modelo no Gensim.
Dê um exemplo de transformação que um modelo pode realizar.

concepts.label: Modelo TF-IDF no Gensim
concepts.description: O modelo TF-IDF transforma vetores bag-of-words ponderando as frequências dos termos pela inversa da frequência nos documentos, dando menos peso a palavras comuns e mais a palavras raras.
coverage_criteria: Explique o efeito do TF-IDF sobre os pesos das palavras.
Compare os pesos de palavras frequentes e raras após aplicar TF-IDF.

concepts.label: Similarity Queries with Gensim
concepts.description: After transforming a corpus with a model (e.g., TF-IDF), Gensim can compute similarity scores between a query document and all documents in the corpus, enabling search and clustering.
coverage_criteria: Explain how to perform a similarity query in Gensim.
Interpret similarity scores from a given output.
Sort documents by relevance using similarity scores.

concepts.label: Gensim Library and Text Preprocessing
concepts.description: Gensim is an open-source NLP library providing tools for text preprocessing and analysis. Key preprocessing steps include tokenizing text with simple_preprocess() or tokenize(), and building a vocabulary with gensim.corpora.Dictionary(), which maps tokens to integer IDs for model training.
coverage_criteria: Explain that Gensim is a Python library for NLP with origins in topic modeling.
Use simple_preprocess() to tokenize text and filter by length.
Create a Dictionary from tokenized documents and explain its role.

concepts.label: Training Word2Vec Models with Gensim
concepts.description: Gensim's Word2Vec class trains word embeddings on preprocessed sentences. Key parameters (e.g., min_count, size, sg, window, hs, negative) control the training, and the resulting model can be saved and loaded for later use.
coverage_criteria: Instantiate a Word2Vec model with a list of tokenized sentences and basic parameters.
List at least four training parameters and explain their effects.
Save and load a trained Word2Vec model using gensim.save() and gensim.load().

concepts.label: Training Data Generation for Word2Vec
concepts.description: How training samples are created for Word2Vec: using a sliding window to form context-target pairs, representing words with one-hot encoding, and the distinction between CBOW and Skip-gram architectures.
coverage_criteria: Given a short text and window size, generate input-output pairs with context and target words.
Explain that each word is represented as a one-hot vector of vocabulary size.
Distinguish CBOW (predict target from context) from Skip-gram (predict context from target).

concepts.label: Análise de Sentimentos
concepts.description: Técnicas para classificar a polaridade de textos, como positivo, negativo ou neutro.
coverage_criteria: Aplicar modelos simples para classificar sentimentos em amostras de texto.

concepts.label: Nearest Neighbor Retrieval using Word Vectors
concepts.description: Finding the most similar words or items in a vector space by computing distances (e.g., cosine similarity) to all candidates and selecting the closest ones. This underlies functions like closest() for color vectors and similar_by_word() for word embeddings.
coverage_criteria: Describe the process of scanning all vectors to find the closest one.
Explain why naive nearest neighbor search is inefficient for large spaces.
Use similar_by_word() to retrieve semantically similar words from a trained Word2Vec model.

concepts.label: Using Pre-trained Word Embeddings
concepts.description: Several publicly available pre-trained word vectors, such as GloVe (300-dimensional) and Google's word2vec model, can be easily loaded via libraries like spaCy or gensim.downloader. These provide ready-to-use semantic spaces without training from scratch.
coverage_criteria: State that GloVe vectors are 300-dimensional and available in spaCy.
Write code to load a pre-trained model using gensim.downloader.load() (e.g., 'word2vec-google-news-300').
Explain the benefit of using pre-trained embeddings for NLP tasks.

concepts.label: Sentence Similarity through Averaged Word Vectors
concepts.description: A sentence can be represented as the average of its word vectors. Cosine similarity between these sentence vectors can then be used to find semantically similar sentences, enabling applications like sentence retrieval.
coverage_criteria: Compute the average word vector for a given sentence.
Explain how sentence vectors allow comparison of longer texts.
Describe using cosine similarity to measure sentence similarity.

concepts.label: Comparing Word Embedding and Feature Extraction Approaches for NLP
concepts.description: Analyzing the differences between NLP systems built using pre-trained word embeddings (e.g., Word2Vec, GloVe) versus traditional feature extraction methods, including trade-offs in dimensionality, semantic capture, and model complexity.
coverage_criteria: Can identify differences in input representation between embedding-based and feature extraction-based NLP models.
Can discuss trade-offs (e.g., dimensionality, semantic capture) between the two approaches.

concepts.label: McCulloch-Pitts neuron model
concepts.description: The first computational model of a neuron proposed by McCulloch and Pitts in 1943, representing neurons as simple electrical circuits with binary outputs.
coverage_criteria: Identify McCulloch and Pitts as the authors of the first formal neuron model in 1943.
Describe the basic idea of a simplified neuron with binary output.

concepts.label: Hebbian learning
concepts.description: The principle that neural connections are strengthened when the pre- and post-synaptic neurons fire together, introduced by Donald Hebb in 1949 and later formalized as a learning rule.
coverage_criteria: State Hebb's postulate: 'neurons that fire together wire together'.
Give one example of a Hebbian-like learning rule.

concepts.label: Perceptron
concepts.description: A single-layer neural network model by Frank Rosenblatt (1958) that computes a weighted sum of inputs, subtracts a threshold, and outputs a binary class; it defines a linear decision boundary.
coverage_criteria: Explain the perceptron architecture: inputs, weights, bias, activation (step function).
State that the perceptron performs binary classification and can learn simple linearly separable patterns.

concepts.label: ADALINE and MADALINE
concepts.description: Early adaptive linear neural networks (ADALINE, MADALINE) developed by Widrow and Hoff (1959) that used adaptive linear elements; MADALINE was the first neural network applied to a real-world problem (echo cancellation).
coverage_criteria: Explain what ADALINE and MADALINE stand for.
Identify echo cancellation as the first real-world application of a neural network (MADALINE).

concepts.label: Minsky & Papert critique and the AI winter
concepts.description: The 1969 book 'Perceptrons' by Minsky and Papert proved the limitations of single-layer perceptrons, leading to a halt in neural network funding and research throughout the 1970s.
coverage_criteria: Explain that Minsky and Papert demonstrated the inability of perceptrons to solve non-linearly separable problems (like XOR), causing a funding freeze.
Define the term 'AI winter' in the context of neural networks.

concepts.label: Hopfield networks and the revival of neural network research
concepts.description: John Hopfield's 1982 paper and the US-Japan Conference on Cooperative Competitive Neural Networks rekindled interest and funding in neural networks, ending the AI winter.
coverage_criteria: State that Hopfield's 1982 approach and the US-Japan conference helped restart neural network funding.
Mention that the conference and the Japanese fifth-generation project spurred renewed investment.

concepts.label: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
concepts.description: A specialized recurrent neural network architecture using gated memory cells (forget, input, output gates) to learn long-term dependencies and mitigate the vanishing gradient problem; introduced by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber in 1997.
coverage_criteria: Explain the purpose of an LSTM: to handle long-term dependencies in sequences.
Name the three gates and their basic roles (forget, input, output).
Contrast LSTM with a simple RNN in terms of memory capability.

concepts.label: Feedforward neural network architecture
concepts.description: A neural network organized into sequential layers (input, hidden, output) where connections flow only forward without cycles; each neuron computes a weighted sum plus bias followed by an activation function.
coverage_criteria: Sketch a diagram of a feedforward network with at least one hidden layer.
Explain the function of weights and biases in a feedforward neuron.

concepts.label: Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) basics
concepts.description: A neural network architecture with feedback connections that pass information from one time step to the next, creating an internal memory suitable for sequential data.
coverage_criteria: Explain how recurrent loops distinguish RNNs from feedforward networks.
Give an example of a task that benefits from recurrent architecture (e.g., language modeling, time series prediction).

concepts.label: Autoencoder
concepts.description: An unsupervised neural network that compresses input into a lower-dimensional representation (encoding) and reconstructs the original input (decoding), useful for dimensionality reduction and feature learning.
coverage_criteria: Sketch the encoder-bottleneck-decoder structure.
Explain how an autoencoder can be used for data compression or denoising.

concepts.label: Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)
concepts.description: A framework where a generator network creates synthetic data and a discriminator network tries to distinguish it from real data; adversarial training improves both.
coverage_criteria: Explain the roles of the generator and discriminator.
Describe the adversarial training process as a two-player game.

concepts.label: Convolutional Neural Networks
concepts.description: CNNs are architectures for grid-structured data (e.g., images) that use convolutional layers to detect spatial features, pooling layers to reduce dimensionality, and fully-connected layers for classification. Output size depends on input, filter, stride, and padding.
coverage_criteria: Describe the operation of a convolutional layer (filter, stride, feature map).
Compute the output size of a convolutional layer given input dimensions, filter size, and padding.

concepts.label: Deep Residual Networks
concepts.description: Deep Residual Networks (DRNs) use skip connections (residual blocks) to allow gradients to flow through very deep architectures, mitigating the vanishing gradient problem and enabling training of networks like ResNet.
coverage_criteria: Explain what a residual block is and why it helps train very deep networks.
Name a well-known residual network architecture.

concepts.label: Perceptron and Its Limitations
concepts.description: The perceptron is a single neuron with step activation: output = step(∑ w_i x_i + b). Its training rule: w = w + η (d - y) x. It only solves linearly separable problems; XOR requires a hidden layer (e.g., two-layer network computing AND and OR).
coverage_criteria: Write the perceptron forward pass and training update rule.
Explain why a single perceptron cannot solve XOR and how a hidden layer enables the solution.

concepts.label: Perceptron Multicamadas
concepts.description: Introdução ao perceptron multicamadas como uma extensão para resolver problemas não-linearmente separáveis.
coverage_criteria: O aluno deve diferenciar um perceptron simples de um multicamadas pela presença de camadas ocultas.
O aluno deve justificar a necessidade de camadas múltiplas para datasets não-lineares.

concepts.label: Backpropagation
concepts.description: The core learning algorithm for neural networks that computes the gradient of the loss function with respect to weights using the chain rule and updates weights in the opposite direction to minimize error.
coverage_criteria: List the four main steps of backpropagation: forward pass, loss computation, backward pass (gradient calculation), weight update.
Explain the role of the chain rule in propagating gradients from output to input layers.

concepts.label: Activation Functions
concepts.description: Non-linear activation functions (sigmoid, tanh, ReLU, step, softmax) applied to neuron outputs introduce non-linearity into the network, enabling learning of complex patterns. The sigmoid maps any real to (0,1); tanh to (-1,1); ReLU outputs max(0,x); step produces binary output.
coverage_criteria: List at least three activation functions with their formulas and typical output ranges.
Explain why non-linear activation functions are necessary in hidden layers.
Compare ReLU with sigmoid in terms of gradient flow and practical usage.

concepts.label: Loss Functions
concepts.description: Loss functions quantify the prediction error during training, guiding weight updates. Mean squared error is used for regression, binary cross-entropy for classification; logistic loss is commonly used for binary classification.
coverage_criteria: Match loss functions (MSE, binary cross-entropy) to the appropriate problem type.
Write the logistic loss formula and explain its intuition.

concepts.label: Overfitting and Regularization
concepts.description: Overfitting occurs when a model learns training noise and fails to generalize; underfitting is the opposite. Dropout is a regularization technique that randomly drops neurons during training to prevent overfitting.
coverage_criteria: Define overfitting and underfitting with examples.
Explain how dropout works and why it reduces overfitting.

concepts.label: Linear Algebra Foundations
concepts.description: Neural network computations rely on linear vector spaces, inner products, norms, and linear transformations. These concepts underpin weight matrices and forward/backward passes.
coverage_criteria: Define a linear vector space and list two axioms.
Compute the dot product of two vectors and explain its role in a neuron's weighted sum.

concepts.label: Gradient Descent Optimization
concepts.description: Gradient descent minimizes the loss by iteratively updating parameters: w = w - η * ∇J. The learning rate η controls step size; bias is an additional parameter; Adam adapts η per parameter; an epoch is one full pass over the dataset.
coverage_criteria: Write the gradient descent update rule for a weight.
Explain the role of the learning rate and describe the advantage of the Adam optimizer.
Define epoch and distinguish it from an iteration over a single sample.

concepts.label: Neural Network Training Implementation
concepts.description: Training involves: forward propagation to compute outputs; random weight initialization to break symmetry; a loop over epochs performing forward, cost, backward, and update steps; layer dimensions determine parameter shapes; caches store intermediate values for backprop.
coverage_criteria: List the steps in one training iteration (forward, cost, backward, update).
Explain why weights are initialized randomly and what happens if they are set to zero.
Describe the purpose of caching in forward propagation.

concepts.label: Data Preparation for Neural Networks
concepts.description: Non-numeric inputs must be encoded (e.g., binary encoding, one-hot encoding) for neural networks. Datasets consist of features (attributes) and a target column, and data often needs to be numeric and normalized.
coverage_criteria: Choose an encoding scheme for a categorical variable (e.g., one-hot encoding) and justify.
Given a CSV, identify the feature columns and the target column.

concepts.label: Implementação Manual vs Bibliotecas
concepts.description: Comparação entre implementar um perceptron do zero e usar scikit-learn, destacando a redução de código e complexidade.
coverage_criteria: O aluno deve listar funções do scikit-learn usadas em substituição à implementação manual.
O aluno deve identificar vantagens e desvantagens de cada abordagem.

concepts.label: Acurácia
concepts.description: Métrica de avaliação que calcula a proporção de predições corretas, variando de 0 a 1.
coverage_criteria: O aluno deve calcular a acurácia a partir de predições e classes reais.
O aluno deve interpretar uma acurácia de 1.0 como separação perfeita para dados linearmente separáveis.

concepts.label: What is Keras?
concepts.description: Keras is a high-level deep learning API, available standalone and integrated into TensorFlow (tf.keras), designed to simplify the implementation of neural networks.
coverage_criteria: Identify Keras as a high-level API for neural networks.
State that Keras is available standalone and as tf.keras.

concepts.label: Keras Backend Flexibility
concepts.description: Keras supports multiple backend computation engines such as TensorFlow, Theano, PlaidML, MXNet, and CNTK, with TensorFlow adopting Keras as its official high-level API.
coverage_criteria: List at least two backend engines supported by Keras.
Explain that TensorFlow has integrated Keras as its official high-level API.

concepts.label: Keras Model Types
concepts.description: Keras provides two primary ways to define a neural network: the Sequential model for linear stacks of layers, and the Functional API for complex architectures with shared layers or multiple inputs/outputs.
coverage_criteria: Differentiate between Sequential and Functional models in Keras.
Give an example of when to use each model type.

concepts.label: Compiling a Keras Model
concepts.description: Before training, a Keras model must be compiled using model.compile() to configure the learning process by specifying a loss function (e.g., categorical_crossentropy), an optimizer (e.g., rmsprop), and metrics (e.g., accuracy).
coverage_criteria: Identify the three main arguments to model.compile() and their purposes.
Choose appropriate loss, optimizer, and metrics for a given classification task.

concepts.label: Training a Keras Model with fit()
concepts.description: The model.fit() method trains the compiled model on training data, with key hyperparameters such as epochs (number of passes over the dataset) and batch_size (samples per gradient update).
coverage_criteria: Write a model.fit() call with the required arguments.
Explain the roles of epochs and batch_size in the training process.

concepts.label: Evaluating a Keras Model on Test Data
concepts.description: After training, model.evaluate() computes the loss and any specified metrics (e.g., accuracy) on a held‑out test set, providing an unbiased estimate of model performance.
coverage_criteria: Write a model.evaluate() call on test data.
Interpret the printed loss and accuracy values.

concepts.label: Making Predictions with Keras Models
concepts.description: Trained Keras models can generate predictions on new data using model.predict() to obtain probability distributions, and np.argmax() (or model.predict_classes()) to get the predicted class labels.
coverage_criteria: Use model.predict() to get predictions on test data.
Apply np.argmax() to convert probabilities to class labels.

concepts.label: Normalizing Pixel Values for Neural Networks
concepts.description: To improve training stability, pixel values of images (originally 0‑255) should be normalized to the [0,1] range by dividing by 255.
coverage_criteria: Explain why pixel normalization is beneficial.
Demonstrate the normalization step in code (dividing by 255).

concepts.label: Reshaping and Flattening Image Data for Dense Layers
concepts.description: Since Dense layers expect 1D input, 2D image arrays must be reshaped into 1D vectors, either manually with .reshape() or by inserting a Flatten layer as the first layer in the model.
coverage_criteria: Perform manual reshaping of image data from 2D to 1D.
Explain how a Flatten layer can replace manual reshaping.

concepts.label: One‑Hot Encoding for Categorical Labels
concepts.description: For multi‑class classification, integer labels must be converted to one‑hot encoded vectors using tf.keras.utils.to_categorical() so that the model output can be compared against a probability distribution.
coverage_criteria: Describe why one‑hot encoding is necessary for categorical crossentropy loss.
Use tf.keras.utils.to_categorical() to transform labels.

concepts.label: Inspecting a Keras Model
concepts.description: Keras provides several methods to inspect a model's architecture and weights, including summary(), get_config(), and get_weights().
coverage_criteria: Call model.summary() to view layer details.
Explain what get_config() and get_weights() return.

concepts.label: Saving and reloading Keras models
concepts.description: How to persist a trained Keras model to an HDF5 file using model.save() and restore it with load_model() from tensorflow.keras.models.
coverage_criteria: Student can write the code to save a model to a .h5 file.
Student can reload a saved model and confirm its architecture.

concepts.label: Fine-tuning with custom optimizer parameters
concepts.description: How to customize the optimizer by instantiating it with specific learning rate and decay values (e.g., RMSprop(lr=0.0001, decay=1e-6)) and compiling the model with it.
coverage_criteria: Student can create an optimizer object with custom parameters.
Student can use the optimizer in model.compile().

concepts.label: Fine-tuning with Early Stopping
concepts.description: How to use the EarlyStopping callback to stop training when a monitored metric (e.g., validation loss) stops improving after a given patience, preventing overfitting.
coverage_criteria: Student can instantiate EarlyStopping with a patience value.
Student can pass the callback to the fit() method.

concepts.label: Keras model building workflow
concepts.description: The sequential pipeline for building a neural network in Keras: import modules, create a Sequential model, add layers, compile with optimizer and loss, fit on data, and make predictions. This high-level process applies to classification tasks.
coverage_criteria: Student can list the steps: define, compile, fit, evaluate, predict.
Student can explain the role of each step in a basic Keras script.

concepts.label: Loading built-in Keras datasets
concepts.description: How to load standard datasets like MNIST, CIFAR-10, Boston Housing, and IMDb directly from tensorflow.keras.datasets, including splitting into training and test sets.
coverage_criteria: Student can list at least three available datasets.
Student can write the code to load one dataset and unpack it into (x_train, y_train), (x_test, y_test).

concepts.label: MNIST dataset characteristics
concepts.description: The MNIST dataset consists of 28x28 grayscale images of handwritten digits 0-9, with 60,000 training and 10,000 test samples. It is a common beginner dataset for deep learning.
coverage_criteria: Student can recall the image size, number of classes, and train/test split.
Student can explain why MNIST is often used as an introductory dataset.

concepts.label: Inspecting data shape and labels
concepts.description: After loading data, how to inspect array shapes (e.g., train_images.shape) and visualize samples using matplotlib to verify the data before modeling.
coverage_criteria: Student can print and interpret the shape of training data and labels.
Student can display a single image using plt.imshow() or plt.matshow().

concepts.label: Sequence padding for RNNs
concepts.description: How to pad variable-length sequences to a fixed length using tensorflow.keras.preprocessing.sequence.pad_sequences, with specification of maxlen, to prepare data for recurrent neural networks.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain why padding is necessary for RNN input.
Student can apply pad_sequences to both training and test sequences.

concepts.label: Standardization with StandardScaler
concepts.description: How to standardize features by scaling them to have zero mean and unit variance using StandardScaler from sklearn.preprocessing, fitting on training data and transforming both train and test sets.
coverage_criteria: Student can fit and transform data with StandardScaler.
Student can distinguish standardization from normalization.

concepts.label: Building an MLP for binary classification
concepts.description: Constructing a Sequential model with Dense layers for binary classification: relu activation for hidden layers and sigmoid for the output layer.
coverage_criteria: Student can create an MLP with the correct activation functions.
Student can explain why sigmoid is suitable for binary output.

concepts.label: Building an MLP for multi-class classification with Dropout
concepts.description: Stacking Dense layers with relu activation, interspersed with Dropout for regularization, and ending with a softmax output layer for multi-class classification.
coverage_criteria: Student can add Dropout layers between Dense layers.
Student can explain why softmax is used for multi-class output.

concepts.label: Building an MLP for regression
concepts.description: Construct a regression neural network using Dense layers without activation on the output to predict continuous values.
coverage_criteria: Student can create a regression MLP by omitting activation on the final Dense layer.
Student can explain why no activation is needed for regression output.

concepts.label: Building a CNN in Keras
concepts.description: Construct a convolutional neural network using Conv2D, Activation, MaxPooling2D, Dropout, Flatten, and Dense layers.
coverage_criteria: Student can stack Conv2D, Activation('relu'), and MaxPooling2D layers.
Student can explain the role of Flatten before the Dense classifier.

concepts.label: Building an RNN with LSTM
concepts.description: Create a recurrent neural network by adding an Embedding layer and an LSTM layer with dropout, followed by a Dense output for binary classification.
coverage_criteria: Student can add Embedding and LSTM layers to a Sequential model.
Student can explain the purpose of dropout and recurrent_dropout in LSTM.

concepts.label: Loading external data from a URL with NumPy
concepts.description: Use urllib.request.urlopen and np.loadtxt to fetch a CSV dataset from a URL and split it into feature matrix and target vector.
coverage_criteria: Student can write the code to open a URL, load its content as a NumPy array, and slice the columns into features and labels.

concepts.label: Text Summarization Objectives
concepts.description: Text summarization aims to condense information from one or more source texts into a shorter version that preserves the main ideas and important content, serving as a tool for accessibility and efficient information retrieval.
coverage_criteria: Student can state the primary goal of text summarization and list its benefits for readers and producers.

concepts.label: Mono-document vs Multi-document Summarization
concepts.description: Summarization can be classified by the number of input documents: mono-document summarization produces a summary from a single text, while multi-document summarization synthesizes information from multiple related documents, often dealing with greater information volume.
coverage_criteria: Student can differentiate between mono-document and multi-document summarization and provide an example scenario for each.

concepts.label: Extractive vs Abstractive Summarization
concepts.description: Extractive summarization selects and concatenates unchanged sentences from the source text, while abstractive summarization may rephrase or generate new sentences, potentially altering structure and meaning, and requiring more complex NLP.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain the difference between extractive and abstractive summarization, and identify which is more complex and why.

concepts.label: Indicative vs Informative Summaries
concepts.description: Indicative summaries provide a vague idea of the content and cannot replace the source, while informative summaries preserve the main content and can act as substitutes, allowing users to understand the subject without reading the full text.
coverage_criteria: Student can distinguish between indicative and informative summaries and explain when each is more appropriate.

concepts.label: Generic vs User-Oriented Summaries
concepts.description: Generic summaries present the most important information without considering the user's background, while user-oriented summaries tailor the content based on the user's knowledge, providing context for novices or novelty for experts.
coverage_criteria: Student can differentiate between generic and user-oriented summaries and describe a scenario where user-oriented would be beneficial.

concepts.label: Supervised vs Unsupervised Summarization
concepts.description: Supervised summarization treats sentence inclusion as a classification task trained on labeled examples, while unsupervised summarization uses pre-defined features and heuristics to determine sentence importance without needing training data.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain the difference between supervised and unsupervised approaches to summarization and give an example of each.

concepts.label: Intermediate Representation in Summarization
concepts.description: The first step of summarization processing is creating an intermediate representation that captures the main aspects of the text, such as topic representations using word frequency tables or more complex indicators.
coverage_criteria: The student can define intermediate representation and describe one common method.

concepts.label: Sentence Scoring for Summarization
concepts.description: After intermediate representation, each sentence receives a score indicating its importance, often based on how well it expresses key topics or a combination of indicator evidence, sometimes using machine learning.
coverage_criteria: The student can explain the purpose of sentence scoring and describe a common method.

concepts.label: Sentence Selection Algorithms
concepts.description: The summarization system selects a set of high-scoring sentences to form a summary, using greedy approaches that recalculate importance considering redundancy, or global optimization maximizing importance and coherence.
coverage_criteria: The student can describe the goal of sentence selection and outline one approach.

concepts.label: Reformulation in Abstractive Summarization
concepts.description: In abstractive summarization, a final reformulation step rewrites or paraphrases the selected content to produce a fluent summary, often using natural language generation.
coverage_criteria: The student can explain when reformulation is applied and its role.

concepts.label: Compression Rate in Summarization
concepts.description: Compression rate defines the size of the summary relative to the source text; e.g., a 60% compression rate means the summary will be 40% of the original length.
coverage_criteria: The student can define compression rate and calculate target summary length.

concepts.label: Extractive Summarization Example with Python and NLTK
concepts.description: An extractive summarization workflow in Python using urllib, BeautifulSoup, NLTK for tokenization and stopword removal, then scoring sentences by word frequency to select the top sentences.
coverage_criteria: The student can list the main steps: fetching data, parsing HTML, tokenizing, removing stopwords, creating frequency distribution, scoring sentences, and selecting top sentences.

concepts.label: BERT Sentence Embeddings and K-Medoid Clustering for Extractive Summarization
concepts.description: Pre-trained BERT models convert sentences into fixed-length embeddings, which are then clustered using K-medoid to select representative sentences as the extractive summary, ensuring selected sentences are actual text excerpts.
coverage_criteria: The student can explain how BERT creates sentence embeddings and how K-medoid clustering selects sentences.
The student can contrast K-means and K-medoid for this task.

concepts.label: Fine-tuning GPT-2 for Abstractive Summarization
concepts.description: GPT-2 is fine-tuned with a multi-loss strategy combining language modeling and multiple-choice prediction, using special tokens like <summarize> and keywords as input, with masked self-attention ensuring auto-regressive generation.
coverage_criteria: The student can describe the two training objectives (language modeling and multiple-choice) and their weighting.
The student can explain the role of special tokens and masked self-attention in the fine-tuning process.

concepts.label: Keyword Extraction for Abstractive Summarization
concepts.description: In the abstractive summarization pipeline, important keywords (nouns and verbs) are automatically extracted using techniques like NLTK POS tagging or fine-tuned BERT, providing a condensed representation for the summarization model.
coverage_criteria: The student can name at least one method for keyword extraction and explain how keywords are used in the summarization input.

concepts.label: Data Scarcity in Domain-Specific Summarization
concepts.description: Low availability of domain-specific data (e.g., only 35k pairs in COVID-19 research vs 286k in general datasets) and rare terminology can hinder effective fine-tuning of large models like BERT and GPT-2.
coverage_criteria: The student can quantify the data size challenge and explain why limited domain data degrades fine-tuning.

concepts.label: Future Direction: Hybrid Extractive-Abstractive Summarization
concepts.description: A suggested future approach is to feed sentences extracted by extractive summarization directly into an abstractive model, potentially improving summary quality by providing richer context.
coverage_criteria: The student can summarize this future work suggestion and discuss one potential benefit.

concepts.label: Feature Extraction in NLP
concepts.description: The process of transforming cleaned text into numerical features that machine learning algorithms can process, a fundamental step in NLP pipelines.
coverage_criteria: Explain why text needs to be converted to numbers for ML models.
List common feature extraction methods (e.g., BoW, TF-IDF, embeddings).
Describe the role of feature extraction in an NLP pipeline.

concepts.label: Implementing Feature Extraction in Python for NLP
concepts.description: Practical implementation of NLP feature extraction pipelines using Python libraries such as scikit-learn, NLTK, and spaCy, including loading text data and applying methods like CountVectorizer.
coverage_criteria: Can write code that loads text data and applies a feature extraction method (e.g., using scikit-learn's CountVectorizer).
Can describe common Python libraries used for NLP feature extraction.

concepts.label: Building a Python Web API to Serve NLP Models
concepts.description: Developing a Python-based web API to serve NLP models, using frameworks like Flask or FastAPI, including steps to wrap a model into a REST endpoint and considerations like latency and data serialization.
coverage_criteria: Can outline steps to wrap an NLP model into a simple REST API using Python.
Can identify challenges in serving NLP models via APIs (e.g., latency, data serialization).

concepts.label: Creating a Basic Flask API Endpoint
concepts.description: Setting up a minimal Flask application by importing Flask, creating an instance, defining a route with @app.route to bind a view function that returns data (e.g., JSON), and running the app. This forms the basis for a simple API endpoint.
coverage_criteria: Can write a minimal Flask app that defines a route returning a string or JSON.
Can explain how the @app.route decorator registers a URL endpoint.

concepts.label: Handling Dynamic URL Parameters and URL Generation in Flask
concepts.description: Using Flask's variable rules to capture dynamic parts of a URL (e.g., <int:user_id>) and employing url_for() to generate URLs for view functions, promoting maintainable and flexible endpoint design.
coverage_criteria: Can write a route with a dynamic path segment and enforce type with converters.
Can use url_for() to generate a URL to a given view function, including passing arguments.

concepts.label: Defining API endpoints with HTTP methods in Flask
concepts.description: Specify allowed HTTP methods with the methods argument to @app.route; use request.method to branch, or use shortcut decorators @app.get/@app.post.
coverage_criteria: Can create a route that handles both GET and POST
Can use request.method to distinguish request types
Can rewrite using separate @app.get and @app.post decorators

concepts.label: NLP Vocabulary: Document, Body, Dictionary, Topic
